ety.text: Originally short for “rifled gun”, referring to the spiral grooves inside the barrel. From Middle English riflen (“to rob, plunder, search through”), from Old French rifler (“to lightly scratch, scrape off, plunder”), from Old High German riffilōn (compare German riffeln (“to score, make grooves in, ripple”), archaic Dutch rijfelen (“to scrape”), Old English rifelan, riflian (“to wrinkle”)), frequentative of Proto-Germanic *rīfaną (compare Old Norse rífa (“to tear, break”)). More at rive.

senses.d: A firearm fired from the shoulder; improved range and accuracy is provided by a long, rifled barrel.
A rifleman.
An artillery piece with a rifled barrel.
A strip of wood covered with emery or a similar material, used for sharpening scythes.
To quickly search through many items (such as papers, the contents of a drawer, a pile of clothing).
ex: She made a mess when she rifled through the stack of papers, looking for the title document.

senses.d: To commit robbery or theft.
To search with intent to steal.
To strip of goods; to rob; to pillage.
ex: Stand, sir, and throw us that you have about ye: / If not, we'll make you sit and rifle you.

senses.d: To seize and bear away by force; to snatch away; to carry off.
ex: Time shall rifle every youthful grace.

senses.d: To add a spiral groove to a gun bore to make a fired bullet spin in flight in order to improve range and accuracy.
To cause (a projectile, as a rifle bullet) to travel in a flat ballistic trajectory.
To move in a flat ballistic trajectory (as a rifle bullet).
ex: The ball rifled off the bat.

senses.d: To dispose of in a raffle.
ex: I've at one throw / Rifled away the diadem of Spain; […]

senses.d: To engage in a raffle.
ex: We'll strike up a drum, set up a tent, call people together, put crowns apiece, let's rifle for her

ety.text: From Old French fuisil, foisil, from Vulgar Latin *focīlis (petra), from Latin focus. Compare Italian fucile.
From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus. Compare French fusil, Friulian fusîl, Piedmontese fusil.
See scoppio (“explosion”), of onomatopoeic origin. Alternatively from Latin stloppus (“sound of a slap”).
Frankish *rīffilōnbor. Old French riflerbor. Middle English riflen English riflebor. Spanish rifle Borrowed from English rifle.
From French fusil, from Vulgar Latin petra (“stone”) + focilis (“of fire”) (flintstone), from focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“fireplace, hearth”). Cognate of English fusillade.

pt:espingarda.gl: long gun (any firearm with long barrel, typically fired while braced against the shoulder)

ety.text: From Italian spingarda, from French espringale (“springald”), from Frankish *springan (“spring, jump”), from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *spr̥ǵʰ.
Borrowed from English rifle, from Middle English, from Old French rifler (“to scrape off, plunder”), from Old Low Franconian Old Dutch *rifillon, frequentative of Proto-Germanic *rīfaną.
From Middle English rift, of North Germanic origin; akin to Danish rift, Norwegian Bokmål rift (“breach”), Old Norse rífa (“to tear”). More at rive.

senses.d: A chasm or fissure.
ex: The Grand Canyon is a rift in the Earth's surface, but is smaller than some of the undersea ones.

senses.d: A lack of cohesion; a state of conflict, incompatibility, or emotional distance.
ex: My marriage is in trouble: the fight created a rift between us and we can't reconnect.

senses.d: A break in the clouds, fog, mist etc., which allows light through.
A shallow place in a stream; a ford.
To form a rift; to split open.
To cleave; to rive; to split.
ex: to the dread rattling thunder / Have I given fire and rifted Jove's stout oak / With his own bolt

senses.d: To belch.

grp.label: break in the clouds, fog, mist etc.

chain.g: to cleave, break up, separate, divide, split, part

ety.text: Attested since the 14th century. Either from Vulgar Latin *findita, feminine of *finditus, as an alternate past participle of Latin findō (normally fissus), or a later formation. Either way equivalent to fendre + -te.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fissūra.

chain.g: schism (a split or separation within a group or organization)

ety.text: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).
